newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire aid force stalled despite HQ decision.
newsitem.headline: Zaire aid force stalled despite HQ decision.

text.p: A multinational force to help refugees missing in eastern Zaire must await the results of negotiations with the government of Zaire before it swings into action, aid workers said on Saturday.

Ambassadors from 14 countries gave the official green light for the Canadian-led force at a meeting in Ottawa on Friday but the organisers have not yet chosen whether to opt for airdrops or for deploying ground troops to escort aid convoys.

More than 20 countries including the United States, France, Britain, Belgium, Senegal and South Africa will contribute to the mission, more likely to comprise 1,000 or 2,000 troops than the 10,000 originally planned.
But the force must get permission from Zaire before it can start helping the hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees still thought to be in eastern Zaire, plus displaced Zaireans.
"It is clear that they (the force) have to get Kinshasa's okay and if they don't, they can't do airdrops and maybe they won't do anything at all," a senior aid worker told Reuters.

No date has been finalised for a key visit to Zaire by the force commander, Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, originally scheduled for Saturday or Sunday, said Major Rod Babiuk, the spokesman for a liaison team in the Rwandan capital Kigali.
"We have to wait and see what conditions Zaire imposes, but it seems clear that Zaire wants intervention with ground troops because that would neutralise the rebels," the aid worker said.
The rebels, known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces, went on the offensive in October against both the Zairean army and Rwandan Hutu militiamen who want the refugees to stay in Zaire.
Up to 600,000 Rwandan Hutus have returned home, mainly from Goma camps, since November 15, but debate continues over the number and location of those still missing and how to help them.
The rebels, who control a swath of eastern Zaire, have argued against multinational ground troops and may set their own conditions for letting them enter the area.
The Rwandan government, whose cooperation would also be useful to the multinational force, maintains there is no need for an international force since most refugees are back home.
Babiuk said Canada had authorised the Ugandan capital Kampala as the forward headquarters and Stuttgart in Germany as the rear headquarters.
"This decision will accelerate the planning process, but still no decision has been taken with regard to airdrops and the deployment of personnel on the ground," Babiuk added.
Asked about plans to send officers into Zaire this weekend on a reconnaissance mission with the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR, he said: "Not yet, (it's) an idea that was floated only."
Around 260 Canadian forward troops are already stationed at Entebbe airport in Uganda and there are 19 in Kigali, but that number is set to increase, the spokesman added.
Up to 1.2 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees fled camps around the east Zairean towns of Goma, Bukavu and Uvira in October following a lightning campaign by the Zairean rebels.
Many aid agencies have dismissed the airdrop option, saying it would be dangerous and ineffective.

"The main complication (with airdrops) is that we don't know who is where and you have to secure the drop zones on the ground for the most vulnerable," said Nina Winquist-Galbe, spokeswoman for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
"You need to go in with ground troops and secure the area anyway for the airdrops," she said.

Refugees continued to return to Rwanda from camps around Bukavu on Saturday, UNHCR said. Around 1,000 per day have come back through Cyangugu since Thursday, according to UNHCR public information officer Mans Nyberg.

"They are coming from the area northwest of Bukavu and they are in very bad physical condition. Basically they have been hiding in the forest. Many of them were forced to flee by the Interahamwe (the Hutu militia)," Nyberg said in a telephone interview from Cyangugu.
